sections.body_en:
The Sages said: Four must give thanks: seafarers who have returned to dry land, desert travelers who have returned to settled land, the sick who have recovered, and prisoners who have been released from prison; and they based their words on the verses of the psalm of thanksgiving in Tehillim 107 (Berakhot 54b). The Sages instituted that they give thanks before a minyan by saying a blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who bestows good things upon the culpable, who has bestowed every goodness upon me" (ha-gomel le-ḥayavim tovot she-gemalani kol tov). That is, although there are sins and flaws in us because of which we may be considered "culpable," nevertheless He, may He be blessed, bestows good things upon us and saves us from dangers. After the blessing, the listeners respond "Amen," and add: "May He [God] who has bestowed every goodness upon you continue to bestow every goodness upon you, Selah" (SA OḤ 219:1-2).

The routine of life greatly interferes with the recognition of all the good that God created in the world, and so at times, instead of thanking God, we complain that it is too hot or too cold, too crowded or too empty, and so on. But a person who sailed on a ship, suffered from the waves and vomited up his insides, when he returns to dry land knows how pleasant and good ordinary life is, and it is fitting that he thank God. And at times a person feels oppressed by social life, which does not satisfy him and perhaps even weighs on him; but when he wanders in the desert, far from his friends, he understands how much society protects him, and how comfortable and good it is to live within an orderly society with basic services, such as water infrastructure, food stores, commerce and health services. Therefore, when he returns to settled land, he must give thanks. Likewise, a healthy person does not always know how to properly appreciate his good condition, and only after he has fallen ill does he come to realize how precious health is, and when he recovers he must give thanks. Likewise, one who was imprisoned is usually a person who did not recognize the value of orderly life, with its limiting aspects, and aspired to more than can be attained in the ordinary way, and sinned against his fellows and was caught and punished. When he is released from his imprisonment, he must give thanks and recognize how wonderful ordinary life is in the world of the Holy One, blessed be He, and regret that he did not recognize this before he sinned. Therefore, in the wording of the blessing we say: "who bestows good things upon the culpable." And even the other three who recite Ha-gomel are considered "culpable" to some degree, for they did not recognize how fitting it is to thank God for the good in routine life (Olat Re'iya vol. 1, pp. 309-312).

The Ha-gomel blessing is unique in that it must be recited in a minyan, and in addition two of them must be Torah scholars, as it is stated in the psalm describing the four who must give thanks (Tehillim 107:32): "Let them exalt Him in the congregation of the people, and praise Him in the assembly of the elders" – "in the congregation of the people" refers to ten, and "in the assembly of the elders" refers to two Torah scholars. As we learned in the previous halakha, the routine of life prevents us from recognizing the value of the life the Creator has granted us. And so we often go about gloomy and irritable, and all sorts of small events cause us displeasure. But those people who left the routine of life, suffered and were endangered, can understand well how good and joyful routine life is. In order to root within us the recognition of the goodness of life, the Sages instituted that a person who for a while lost the pleasantness of his ordinary life should thank God, before a minyan that includes two Torah scholars, for the good He has bestowed upon him; and through this, both the one reciting the blessing and the listeners will be aroused to contemplate the value of ordinary life more, and God's name will be sanctified in the world.

If one erred and recited the blessing not in a minyan, some say that he has fulfilled his obligation (Ritva), and some say that he has not fulfilled it (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona and Meiri); therefore, it is good that he recite the blessing again without God's name and kingship before ten (SA 219:3). And if he is able to hear another person reciting Ha-gomel, he should ask him to have in mind to fulfill the obligation on his behalf with his blessing.

Ideally, there should be two Torah scholars present at the recitation of Ha-gomel, but if there are not two Torah scholars there, this does not invalidate it. But the minyan is indispensable, and when there is no minyan – one should not recite the blessing. When necessary, the one reciting the blessing may also be counted toward the minyan.1

notes_en.en: The Rishonim disagree as to whether the minyan is indispensable. According to the Ra'ah, Ritva and Tur – it is not indispensable. And according to Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, Meiri, Ha-mikhtam and Ha-me'orot – it is indispensable. SA 219:3 mentioned both opinions, and in the second "some say," which according to the rules of the SA is the halakha, he wrote that the minyan is indispensable. Some of the Aḥaronim are inclined to rely after the fact on the opinion that the minyan is not indispensable (Baḥ; Knesset Ha-gedola; Ateret Tzvi). MB 219:8 also leans toward their view, and wrote, based on the Ra'ah, that if one cannot recite the blessing in a minyan within thirty days, he should recite it without a minyan. Similarly, the Knesset Ha-gedola wrote that a woman may recite the blessing before women or one man; this was cited by Birkei Yosef 2 and MB 3. But the opinion of most Aḥaronim is that the minyan is indispensable (Levush; Eliya Rabba; Ḥayei Adam; Maḥatzit Ha-shekel; Magen Giborim; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav; Ḥesed La-alafim; Ben Ish Ḥai; Arukh Ha-shulḥan; and others). Therefore, one should not recite the blessing without a minyan of men. So too wrote Ḥazon Ovadia p. 342, Birur Halakha by Rabbi Zilber, Kama, p. 185, and Piskei Teshuvot 219:15. Ideally, it is good that there be ten without the one reciting the blessing, for this is the opinion of several poskim (Maharanaḥ; Ḥayei Adam). When necessary, one may also count the one reciting the blessing, in accordance with the opinion of most poskim (Halakhot Ketanot; Ḥida; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav; MB 6).

sections.title_en: The Time for the Ha-gomel Blessing
sections.body_en:
It is proper to recite Ha-gomel within three days of the event over which one is reciting the blessing. However, after the fact, even if much time has passed, one has not lost the blessing, for it has no limited time (SA 219:6). But if the matter has already been forgotten from the heart, even when he remembers he should not recite the blessing (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 219:7).

The custom is to recite Ha-gomel standing (Rambam; Baḥ 219:1). Men customarily recite Ha-gomel close to the Torah reading, and when possible, the custom is to call up to the Torah the one who must recite Ha-gomel. But one should not wait more than three days in order to recite the blessing close to the Torah reading. For example, one who was saved from a terror attack on Monday should try to recite the blessing by Wednesday, which is the third day after the attack. And he should not wait until the Torah reading on Thursday, which is the fourth day after the attack (MA; MB 219:20).

The time for the Ha-gomel blessing is after the trouble has completely ended. Therefore, a person who has risen from his illness and returned to his work but is still in the process of recovery should recite the blessing after the recovery is complete (MB 219:2).2

notes_en.en: Some say that just as the thanksgiving offering was brought in the daytime, so Ha-gomel must be recited specifically in the daytime (Sedeh Yitzḥak; Ben Ish Ḥai). Some say that ideally one recites the blessing at night (Malbim). And some say that men, who customarily recite the blessing at the Torah reading, should ideally recite the blessing in the daytime, but women may ideally recite the blessing at night (Tzitz Eliezer 13:17; Ḥazon Ovadia, Berakhot p. 347).

sections.body_en:
A sick person who recovered recites Ha-gomel only if there was danger in his illness that justifies desecrating Shabbat. Admittedly, in the past, according to Sephardic custom, every sick person who was forced to lie in bed would recite Ha-gomel (SA 219:8). However, this was because in the past there was a concern of danger in almost every illness, since they did not know whether it was influenza or heart disease, mild dehydration or dangerous diabetes. But now that medical science has developed, and it is possible to diagnose the patient's condition and determine whether there was a concern of danger in his illness, one should recite Ha-gomel only over an illness in which there was a certain danger that justifies desecrating Shabbat.3

Over surgery under local anesthesia one should not recite Ha-gomel, for there is no danger in it. But over surgery under general anesthesia, in light of the seriousness with which general anesthesia is regarded medically today, one should recite the blessing.4

notes_en.en:
It is clear that according to the Rema, one recites the blessing only over an illness involving mortal danger. However, seemingly, according to the custom of those of Sephardic descent, every sick person who was forced to lie in bed must recite the blessing, as stated in SA 219:8: "For every illness one must recite the blessing, even if it is not a dangerous illness nor an internal wound; rather, whoever took to bed and got up, because he is like one who was brought up to the scaffold to be judged. And there is no difference between one who has a chronic ailment that comes from time to time and one for whom it is not chronic." So too wrote Kaf Ha-ḥayim 219:46; Ḥazon Ovadia p. 371; Or Le-Tziyon vol. 2, 14:44, that every sick person who needed to lie in bed must recite the blessing. However, it seems that the Sephardic poskim were speaking of an illness in which there is a certain danger, for they based themselves on the words of the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 4:4): "All roads are presumed to be dangerous … all illness is presumed to be dangerous." And so it is implied by the words of the Rambam, Ramban and Rashba, as explained in the Tur and Beit Yosef there, that in every illness there is a certain danger, "like one who was brought up to the scaffold," that perhaps in the end he will die. And even if it is a chronic ailment that comes from time to time, there may be danger in it, as the Beit Yosef cited from a responsum of the Rashba (1:82): "On the contrary, whatever is chronic is more severe. And although a miracle was performed for him many times and he was saved from it, Heaven had mercy on him, and a miracle does not happen at every moment (Megilla 7b)." And so we learn from a responsum of Rav Hai Gaon (cited in the Arukh), that there is an aspect of danger in illness. Therefore, one who recovers from ordinary illnesses that are known to involve no danger, even though he lay in bed, should not recite the blessing. And "go out and see what the people are doing" – this is the practice of those of Sephardic descent. Admittedly, one could interpret that the SA ruled to recite the blessing even over an illness that involves no danger, as several of the great poskim ruled; but besides the principle that "in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient," one should prefer the interpretation that narrows the dispute, according to which all agree that without mortal danger one does not recite the blessing, and their entire dispute in the past concerned one who was forced to lie in bed because of his illness without it being known what his illness was and whether there was danger in it. It should be added that in recent generations we have become more pampered, and many lie in bed because of illnesses that in the past were considered mere aches that do not require lying down. And perhaps this is why the Ben Ish Ḥai (Ekev 7) ruled that only one who lay in bed for three days should recite Ha-gomel. Admittedly, many wrote that one recites the blessing even if he lay in bed less than three days (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 219:46; Ḥazon Ovadia p. 371; Or Le-Tziyon vol. 2, 14:44); however, one may say that they were speaking of an illness involving mortal danger.
If, because of doubt, a sick person was driven to the hospital on Shabbat, and it turned out that the patient was not in danger – although they drove him in accordance with halakha, for even a doubtful danger to life overrides Shabbat – since in fact it turned out that there was no danger in his illness, he should not recite Ha-gomel.

The poskim disagree regarding the law of one who sinned and attempted suicide and remained alive. Some say that he should not recite the blessing, for the whole purpose of the blessing is to give thanks for rescue from natural dangers, and not for rescue from things that a person caused himself intentionally. In addition, how would he dare to thank God in public for rescue from his sin?! Such a person is not blessing but blaspheming (Maḥazik Berakha 219:1; Yeḥaveh Da'at 4:14; Tzitz Eliezer 10:25:23). And some say that he should recite the blessing, for in the end he was in danger and was saved (Lev Ḥayim 3:53). In practice, it is fitting that he hear the blessing from another and ask him to have in mind to fulfill the obligation on his behalf. And of course, he should do great repentance for his sin.

sections.title_en: A Woman After Childbirth, Women and Minors in the Ha-gomel Blessing
sections.body_en:
A woman who has given birth must recite Ha-gomel after she has regained her strength from the birth, for in every birth there is a certain danger, as evidenced by the fact that Shabbat is desecrated in order to care for a woman giving birth. Usually, after seven days the woman who has given birth regains her strength and can recite Ha-gomel. And sometimes her weakness continues for thirty days, in which case she should recite the blessing after thirty days.

In many places women were not careful to recite Ha-gomel, because for reasons of modesty they felt uncomfortable standing before ten men and reciting Ha-gomel (MB 219:3). Some suggested that the woman stand in the women's section, and her husband recite Ha-gomel on her behalf, and she respond "Amen" after him (MB 219:17). However, some say that a husband should not recite the blessing in place of his wife (Beit Yosef), and therefore this suggestion should not be used.

Therefore, a woman who must recite Ha-gomel should come to the synagogue for prayer and inform the gabbai that she must recite Ha-gomel, and at the appropriate time the gabbai will signal the congregation to wait in silence, and the woman will recite Ha-gomel from the women's section, and the congregation will respond "Amen" after her. If it is convenient for her, it is preferable that she come to a prayer service that includes the Torah reading and recite the blessing after the reading. And if ten men happen to be present for her in another place, such as a woman who has given birth at the brit mila of her son, she should recite the blessing before them and will not need to come to the synagogue.5

According to many, a minor who was saved from danger does not recite the blessing, since the wording of the blessing is "who bestows good things upon the culpable," that is, although the one who was in danger deserved punishment, God bestowed kindness upon him. Whereas a minor is not yet punished for his sins, and if a disaster befell him, it is because of the sin of his parents, and perhaps even through their direct fault for not watching over him properly, and it is not fitting that he say of his parents that they are "culpable" (Maharam Mintz 14; MA; Knesset Ha-gedola; MB 219:3). And although some maintain that a minor who has reached the age of education must recite the blessing (Laḥmei Toda; Birkei Yosef; Ḥazon Ovadia), since there is doubt in the matter, he should not recite the blessing (Ben Ish Ḥai; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 2).

notes_en.en: However, after an abortion or a curettage, although it is performed under full anesthesia, women do not customarily recite Ha-gomel because of embarrassment. For we have learned that human dignity is so great that it overrides a negative commandment of the Torah, that is, the negative commandment of "you shall not turn aside" from the enactments that the Sages instituted, and the Ha-gomel blessing is of rabbinic origin. (Furthermore, this procedure is among the lightest of the treatments that require full anesthesia.) And perhaps this is the reason that many women did not recite Ha-gomel in the past: because of the customs of modesty, they were embarrassed to recite the blessing before men. But today, when it is not customary to be so embarrassed, the claim of embarrassment does not exempt women from the Ha-gomel blessing, except in special cases such as a curettage.

sections.title_en: Desert Travelers and Those Traveling on Roads
sections.body_en:
The Sages instructed desert travelers to recite Ha-gomel. In the days of the Rishonim, the custom in Spain was that even those traveling from city to city recited Ha-gomel, whereas in Ashkenaz and France the custom was to recite the blessing only if the road was known to be dangerous, where robbers or beasts of prey were common (SA 219:7).

Some say, accordingly, that according to the custom of those of Sephardic descent, even one who travels today by car for the distance of a parsa's walk, that is, 72 minutes, recites Ha-gomel. And a person who traveled from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv and returned to Jerusalem, since altogether he traveled more than 72 minutes that day, recites Ha-gomel (Netivei Am 219; Yabi'a Omer 1:13; 6:48:9). On the other hand, some say that one recites Ha-gomel only after a journey of 72 minutes in a place empty of people, like a desert; but over travel on the roads of the Land – one should not recite the blessing, since other cars travel on the road, and there is always a settled place less than 72 minutes' drive away, and therefore one who travels on the roads of the Land is not considered a desert traveler (Or Le-Tziyon vol. 2, 14:42; Mekor Ḥayim by Rabbi Ḥayim David [Halevi] 94:3).

Moreover, the Ha-gomel blessing was instituted for rare events, and according to many, only one who would be required to bring a thanksgiving offering recites the blessing, and it is inconceivable that Ha-gomel would be recited over routine travel. Therefore, it seems in practice that one should not recite the blessing over travel on paved roads in developed countries, including the roads of Judea and Samaria.6

notes_en.en: Although road accidents are very dangerous, relative to the length of time people spend traveling, this is a low danger that does not justify the Ha-gomel blessing. As of 5779 (2019), the chance of being involved in a road accident on a 100 km journey (about 72 minutes) is 23 in a million, and only in 15% of cases will it be a severe or fatal accident (according to data of the Central Bureau of Statistics). Statistically, there is no great danger in this

sections.title_en: Flying in an Airplane and Sailing on a Ship
sections.body_en:
In recent generations the question has arisen whether those who fly in an airplane are considered like desert travelers who must recite Ha-gomel. Some say that they are not like desert travelers. In addition, flying today is no more dangerous than traveling by car, and just as one does not recite the blessing after a car journey, so one should not recite the blessing after a flight (Ḥelkat Ya'akov 2:9; Devar Yehoshua, Berakhot 9; Rabbi Goren; Rabbi Ḥayim David Halevi, Aseh Lekha Rav 6:16). In contrast, many poskim ruled to recite Ha-gomel after a flight. Rabbi Feinstein explained (Iggerot Moshe OḤ 2:59) that the Ha-gomel blessing was instituted for a person's departure from the ordinary order into a dangerous situation, for it is not natural for a person to remain in the air and not fall, and since there is a rescue from danger here, one should recite Ha-gomel afterward (so too wrote Ketzot Ha-shulḥan [?], and Halikhot Shlomo 23:5). However, several poskim wrote that one should recite the blessing only after a flight of at least 72 minutes (Tzitz Eliezer 11:13, and Yeḥaveh Da'at vol. 2, 26).

In practice, it seems that one should not recite the blessing, since the Ha-gomel blessing was instituted for an exceptional situation, whereas flights have become a routine event that is no more dangerous than traveling by car. However, if a person who is not accustomed to flying feels anxiety during his flight and wishes to recite the blessing – he may rely on those who maintain that one must recite the blessing.

Similarly, the poskim disagree regarding sailing on the safe ships of our times. In practice, it seems that if no especially dangerous event occurred during the voyage, one should not recite Ha-gomel over an ordinary voyage.7

notes_en.en:
Or Le-Tziyon vol. 2, 14:43, and Birkat Hashem vol. 4, 6:21, wrote that one should recite the blessing. On the other hand, Devar Yehoshua, Hilkhot Berakhot 9, wrote not to recite the blessing. It is reasonable that all those who wrote in the past not to recite the blessing over short voyages, because there is no danger in them, would say today not to recite the blessing even over long voyages on the safe ships of our times; among them: the Ḥida in Le-David Emet 23:9; Minḥat Yitzḥak 4:11; and see Piskei Teshuvot 219:2. One should also add the opinion of those who maintain that even seafarers recite the blessing only if they encountered danger (Yad Ha-melekh, Hilkhot Berakhot 10:8). I did not add that if the voyager is afraid he should recite the blessing, as with a flight, since those who sail today are either professionals such as sailors, who are not afraid, or people sailing for pleasure, who, since they chose this, do not recite the blessing.
Extreme sports: It seems that one who chooses to go on a trip in the desert or the jungle, or to swim or surf in the depths of the sea, or to do other dangerous activities within the framework of "extreme sports" that people do for pleasure, such as gliding, parachuting, rappelling and the like – as long as the activity proceeded in order without special danger – should not recite the blessing, since it is an event that he chose to do for his pleasure, and presumably he prepared for it properly in order to prevent dangers. And if he chose to do a dangerous activity, he transgressed the mitzva to guard one's life (see Peninei Halakha: Likutim II 9:7), and consequently there is no room for him to recite the blessing over it (similar to what is explained in note 4 regarding one who attempts suicide). However, it seems that if during that dangerous and forbidden activity a mishap occurred that added significant danger beyond what he had planned – he recites the blessing, for he did not enter this danger willingly.

sections.title_en: One Who Was Saved from Danger or from an Accident
sections.body_en:
The Sages mentioned four who must recite Ha-gomel: seafarers, desert travelers, a sick person who recovered and a prisoner who was released (Berakhot 54b). The poskim disagree on the question of whether one who was saved from other dangers as well – for example, robbers or terrorists attacked him in the city, or a wall fell on him, or he was saved from a fire – must recite Ha-gomel.

Some say that he does not recite Ha-gomel, since this blessing was instituted only for the four kinds of danger that were mentioned (R. David Abudarham in the name of Rabbi Gershon). And the opinion of most poskim is that anyone who is saved from danger must thank God with the Ha-gomel blessing (Ramban; Meiri; Ri'az; Rivash; Tashbetz; and others). And so in practice is the custom of those of Ashkenazic descent and some of those of Sephardic and Mizraḥi descent (MB 219:32; from Yemen, Shetilei Zeitim 16; from Algeria, Responsa Beit Yehuda, Ayash, 6; from Turkey, Emet Le-Ya'akov and Responsa Lev Ḥayim, Palagi, 3:53; from Morocco, Shemesh U-magen vol. 3, OḤ 63:10).

According to the custom of some of those of Sephardic descent, since the matter is disputed, anyone who is saved from a danger that is not included in the four kinds of danger the Sages mentioned should say Ha-gomel without God's name and kingship (SA 219:9; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 52; Ḥazon Ovadia). It seems that a traveler who was in a dangerous accident or terror attack and was saved, even according to this custom, recites Ha-gomel, for since the danger occurred on the road, that road became dangerous for him, and travelers on dangerous roads are among the four for whom the Sages instituted the blessing. Likewise, one who was bitten by a dangerous snake is considered a dangerously ill person who recovered, and according to all opinions he recites the blessing over his rescue.

The determination of whether there was danger in the accident or in the attack depends on the judgment of reasonable people: if in their opinion there was danger in it, one should recite the blessing. And if there was no danger – one should not recite the blessing, even though the person felt great fear. Therefore, for example, one who passed near a snake, or who did not pay attention and was almost run over, since in fact he did not enter danger – should not recite the blessing. And when the situation is doubtful, for example, he was in a moderate accident, the feeling of the person who was in the event is decisive: if he felt danger and time passed until he calmed down – he recites the blessing, and if not – he should not recite the blessing.

Soldiers who engage in security activity that involves risk, since they are considered like travelers whose activity involves danger, must recite Ha-gomel. However, they should recite the blessing after the dangerous activity ends, because one recites the blessing only after being completely saved from the danger – like desert travelers whose journey lasted months, who would recite the blessing after the end of their journey.

Therefore, a combat soldier in regular service should recite the blessing at the end of his years of service, and his blessing covers all the risks he went through during the security activity and the training. And a combat soldier in the reserves whose service involved risk should recite the blessing at the end of his reserve service. Soldiers who, in the course of their routine security activity, took part in a battle or a dangerous operation should recite Ha-gomel immediately after they return safely to their routine activity. And at the end of their military service, they should recite Ha-gomel again for their security activity that continued afterward (see Meshiv Milḥama vol. 2, no. 134).

The Sages said that one of the four who must recite Ha-gomel is one who has been released from prison. The question is whether one must recite Ha-gomel even after imprisonment in jail in developed countries. In practice, a prisoner who sat in jail, and the imprisonment shook his soul, must recite Ha-gomel. And although there was no mortal danger in his imprisonment, since the imprisonment shook his soul and aroused great fears in his heart – lest he lose his freedom and lest they abuse and humiliate him – he must give thanks for his release with the Ha-gomel blessing. But if the imprisonment did not shake his soul, and there was no danger whatsoever in it, one should not recite the blessing.

One who was kidnapped by terrorists or robbers who threatened his life, although he was not imprisoned by a government or authority, since in fact he was a prisoner in mortal danger, must recite Ha-gomel when he is released.8

notes_en.en:
Regarding ordinary imprisonment, one might seemingly say that according to Ashkenazic custom, as long as there was no mortal danger in it, even if it lasted many years – one should not recite Ha-gomel, and only according to Sephardic custom would one recite the blessing. However, in practice, a large majority of the poskim, of both Sephardic and Ashkenazic descent, wrote that even one who was imprisoned over a monetary matter must recite the blessing when he is released. As Rav Hai Gaon wrote: "And as for one imprisoned, most of the time he is imprisoned over money, and his danger is not so great." So too wrote R. Yosef Ibn Migash; Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona; Malbushei Yom Tov 1; Netiv Ḥayim; Pe'ulat Tzaddik 3:229; Eliya Rabba 2; Birkei Yosef 4; Ma'amar Mordekhai 2; Ḥesed La-alafim 7; Magen Giborim, Elef Ha-magen 3; Ben Ish Ḥai, Ekev 9; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 5; Minḥat Pittim; Da'at Torah; and others. And even the Leket Yosher, MA 1, and Ḥayei Adam 65:6, who wrote that one who was imprisoned over monetary matters should not recite the blessing, may have meant the detention of wealthy people, whose jailers gave them good conditions until they paid their debt. But regarding sitting in an ordinary jail for a prolonged or unknown period, which involves both extremely great suffering and a trace of danger – both from the harm caused by the other prisoners, some of whom are violent criminals, and from the emotional shock that may endanger his life – it is possible that they would agree that one should recite Ha-gomel.
That is, the level of risk is not the only criterion for the Ha-gomel blessing; rather, whoever has gone through a shaking and traumatic event that involved a trace of danger recites Ha-gomel. Usually, a traumatic event is measured by the danger it involves (as they disagreed regarding roads and illnesses in the past, as explained above in note 3 and in halakha 6); however, imprisonment, even if it is over monetary matters, in which the danger to life is slight, can be very traumatic and shaking, to the point that as a result a person may be endangered. As the Maharitz wrote in Pe'ulat Tzaddik 3:229: "In any case there is a little danger, for he stands in fear until he leaves the trouble." Similarly wrote the Netiv Ḥayim on SA 219:1. And as I wrote at the end of halakha 7, in our current situation, where there are still people who are not accustomed to flying, and it arouses in them the fear that they may fall to their death, it is possible that they should recite Ha-gomel afterward, in accordance with the widespread custom in the previous generation.
From BHL 219:1, s.v. "ḥavush," it is implied that for less than three days in jail one should not recite the blessing. However, it seems that if he was very afraid, because he did not know when he would be released or the interrogators threatened him, he recites the blessing.
One who chose to go to prison – for example, he was offered to pay a fine or to sit in prison for two months – according to Birkei Yosef and Ben Ish Ḥai, although he is at fault in this, nevertheless the Sages did not distinguish in this matter, and he recites the blessing. And according to Sha'arei Teshuva 219:2, he should not recite the blessing with God's name and kingship. And so it is proper to practice, because of the doubt.
The routine of life greatly interferes with the recognition of all the good that God created in the world, and so at times, instead of thanking God, we complain that it is too hot or too cold, too crowded or too empty, and so on. But a person who sailed on a ship, suffered from the waves and vomited up his insides, when he returns to dry land knows how pleasant and good ordinary life is, and it is fitting that he thank God. And at times a person feels oppressed by social life, which does not satisfy him and perhaps even weighs on him; but when he wanders in the desert, far from his friends, he understands how precious society is to him, and how comfortable and good it is to live within an orderly society with basic community services, such as water infrastructure, food stores, commerce and health services. Therefore, when he returns to settled land, he must give thanks. Likewise, a healthy person does not always know how to properly appreciate his good condition, and only after he has fallen ill does he come to realize how precious health is, and when he recovers he must give thanks. And so too regarding one who was imprisoned: often this is a person who did not recognize the value of orderly life, with its limiting aspects, and aspired to more than can be attained in the ordinary way, and sinned against his fellows and was caught and punished. And when he is released, he must give thanks and recognize how wonderful ordinary life is in the world of the Holy One, blessed be He, and he must regret that he did not recognize this before he sinned. Therefore, in the wording of the blessing we say: "who bestows good things upon the culpable." And even the other three who recite Ha-gomel are considered "culpable" to some degree, for they did not previously recognize how fitting it is to thank God for the good in routine life (Olat Re'iya vol. 1, pp. 309-312).
